Why Leaves Change Color
Leaves are green because of chlorophyll, which helps trees turn sunlight into food. Other colors, yellow and orange, are in the leaf all summer, but the green hides them. As autumn days shorten, trees stop making chlorophyll. The green fades, and the hidden yellows show through. Reds are different: many trees make red pigments only in fall, especially after sunny days and cool nights. That is why a dry, bright autumn often brings the most brilliant reds.

No one expected the after-school code club to fill the library. Then Samira posted a flyer that said "Build a game in six weeks — no experience needed." Twenty students showed up. Some had never typed a loop. By week three, pairs were debugging each other's projects, and the librarian had to ask them to whisper. On demo day, a maze game froze twice — and the room still applauded, because everyone recognized the hours behind the glitch.

Glacier Pace
Glaciers look still in photographs, yet they move. Gravity pulls their ice downhill a few inches — or a few feet — each day. Rocks trapped in the ice scrape the valley floor, carving U-shaped valleys over thousands of years. When a glacier melts back, it leaves ridges of debris called moraines. Hikers who stand on a moraine are standing on a timeline written in stone and dirt.

The Quiet Car
The 7:42 train had one car labeled QUIET. No phone calls, no speaker music, headphones only. Mira chose it so she could finish a chapter before school. A tourist once asked, loudly, why everyone looked so serious. The conductor pointed to the sign and smiled. Mira realized the quiet was not empty — it was full of people protecting a little space to think.
